column3: It directly joins a true sign from the Lord with the demand that Pharaoh release the Children of Israel, making it the closest parallel to the focus.
It contrasts the fear that following guidance loses one's land with the focus's presentation of guidance as the path of safety.
Noah's public commission as a clear warner supplies a broader model for the messengers' authorized address to Pharaoh.
It gives the same concise demand that the Children of Israel be sent with the messenger.
The immediately preceding instruction sends Musa and his brother with God's signs and establishes the mission continued in the focus.
It places clear proofs before culpability and punishment, clarifying the evidentiary role of the sign brought to Pharaoh.
It closely parallels the two messengers approaching Pharaoh and declaring their commission from the Lord.
The next ayah states the consequence for denying and turning away from the guidance offered in the focus.
A believer in Pharaoh's setting calls his people to follow him toward right conduct, providing a contextual counterpart to following guidance.
It explicitly frames sending a messenger and following divine signs as the basis for responsibility before punishment.
The designation of manifest book-verses only broadly supports the focus's appeal to a divine sign.
It closely connects divine guidance with the abode of peace, making the focus's peace upon followers of guidance more explicit.
Jesus's mission to the Children of Israel with a sign from his Lord parallels the focus's messenger, people, and sign pattern.
The immediately preceding command identifies Pharaoh's transgression as the reason for the mission announced in the focus.
Elijah's inclusion among the messengers gives only a general prophetic parallel after more specific mission texts.
It links Musa, guidance, and the Children of Israel, though it describes the later inheritance of the Book rather than the demand for release.
It supplies the required gentle mode of speech for the confrontation whose message is delivered in the focus.
It shows that rejecting a recognized messenger and clear proofs blocks guidance, a contrary response to the focus's offered path.
The brothers' request to send Benjamin with them does not clarify the prophetic demand to release Israel.
It names the rescue of the Children of Israel from humiliating torment, the outcome sought by the focus's demand.
It distinguishes the one who guides to truth as worthy of following, supporting the focus's criterion of following guidance.
The brothers' deceptive request to take Joseph away has no focused relation to Musa's emancipatory demand.
The messengers' fear of Pharaoh immediately precedes and explains the high-risk address formulated in the focus.
The refusal of a call to submission supplies a broad contrary response, but adds little beyond the focus's own guidance language.
Musa's concern about speech and his request that Harun be sent explains why the focus speaks in the dual form.
Pharaoh construes Musa's message as an attempt to expel his people from the land, directly exposing his resistance to Israel's release.
Its compelled surrender is contrast evidence, not the peaceful following of guidance offered in the focus.
God's answer with truth and best explanation only generally supports the truth-bearing sign claimed in the focus.
The account of households and provision does not add a focused route to the mission before Pharaoh.
Abraham and his son's submission gives a distant example of voluntary obedience, but not the focus's public guidance and release demand.
It records the eventual inheritance of the oppressed Children of Israel and destruction of Pharaoh's works, supplying the mission's outcome.
God's reassurance that He hears and sees directly answers the fear before the focus's address to Pharaoh.
The sending of the she-camel as a test does not clarify the messenger's demand, sign, or guidance in the focus.
It identifies revelation as insight, guidance, and mercy, supporting the character of the sign and guidance presented to Pharaoh.
The later question to the Samiri does not illuminate the immediate mission to Pharaoh.
Guidance and good news for believers gives a compact general counterpart to peace for those who follow guidance.
It explicitly states that following divine guidance prevents going astray and distress, closely explaining the focus's promise of peace.
A messenger's completed delivery of what he was sent with clarifies the accountability carried by the focus's declaration.
The assertion that Muhammad is among the messengers is a general parallel to Musa and Harun's messenger identity.
It makes the sending of a messenger who recites signs a condition before destruction, reinforcing the procedural logic already present in the focus.
The warning to Adam about exile is not a focused neighbour to the demand made to Pharaoh.
It contrasts an earlier, possible response to a divine call with later humiliation, loosely sharpening the focus's peace-versus-rejection fork.
It explicitly compares a messenger sent to Pharaoh with a later messenger, confirming Pharaoh as a paradigm of response to a mission.
Musa's private prayer for provision does not explain his later public commission or Israel's release.
Its greeting of peace after perseverance gives an eschatological counterpart to the focus's peace upon followers of guidance.
Jesus's declaration of peace across birth, death, and resurrection offers a related but less direct use of peace.
Musa's request to make Harun a partner in his affair directly grounds the joint messenger voice of the focus.
A gentle invitation to follow toward a straight path parallels the focus's linkage of following and guidance.
The irreversible arrival of punishment supplies only a distant contrast to the focus's warning before judgment.
It distinguishes divine ownership of signs from the messenger's clear warning, clarifying the status of the sign claimed in the focus.
Lot's identity as a messenger gives only a general parallel already supplied by closer prophetic mission texts.
It preserves God's authority over punishment and forgiveness, relevant to the focus's prohibition of torment only at a broad level.
Adam's provision in the garden does not clarify the Pharaoh mission.
The inability of persistent transgressors to receive forgiveness or guidance offers a broad contrary outcome, but not the focus's immediate scene.
Noah's call for his son to join the saved party provides a limited rescue-and-following parallel.
The succession of prophecy and Book through Noah and Abraham provides general background for Musa's messenger role.
Jonah's messenger identity is a remote prophetic parallel with no added detail about the focus's message.
The angels' arrival with the disputed punishment does not clarify the focus's guidance or liberation demand.
The completion of Adam's garden provision has no focused relation to the mission before Pharaoh.
It states that messengers deliver their Lord's messages, clarifying the entrusted transmission embodied by Musa and Harun.
It identifies resistance to a human messenger as an obstacle to faith after guidance arrives, a relevant counterpoint to Pharaoh's reception.
Human ownership of livestock does not illuminate the release of an oppressed people.
Following divine pleasure versus returning with wrath is a broad moral fork, less specific than following guidance in the focus.
The direct command to follow what is revealed from the Lord closely supports the focus's call to follow guidance.
Musa's request for a minister from his family is an earlier step toward the two-person commission in the focus.
It makes a more-guiding divine book the criterion to be followed, reinforcing the focus's relation between divine source and guidance.
It explicitly links following God's good pleasure to paths of peace, emergence from darkness, and straight guidance.
Secret obedience to those who hate revelation contrasts with following divine guidance and shows an alternative allegiance.
Opposition to God and His messenger gives a broad negative counterpart to receiving the messengers' appeal.
It contrasts retreat after God has guided with being called back to guidance and submission, strongly illuminating the focus's following formula.
The Lord's unfailing knowledge gives only distant support to the authority of the message delivered to Pharaoh.
Noah's sending to warn before painful punishment parallels the pre-punishment messenger function in the focus.
Pharaoh's demand for a sign from Musa immediately sets up the proof-bearing confrontation represented by the focus.
The succession of messengers and the mixed response of followers supplies only broad prophetic context.
Universal submission, willing or unwilling, only distantly contrasts with the focus's voluntary following of guidance.
A prophet is commanded through revelation to follow a prior upright way, giving a secondary revelation-and-following parallel.
The instruction concerning Musa's staff belongs to the sign sequence but adds little after the mission context is established.
The sending of birds for punishment is not a useful parallel to the sending of human messengers or guidance.
The demand that a human claimant produce a sign parallels Pharaoh's need to confront the sign brought in the focus.
Recognition through the tone of speech does not clarify the focus's message, sign, or response.
The greeting of peace upon all messengers supplies a direct lexical and thematic counterpart to the focus's peace formula.
It describes turning away from the Lord's signs and refusing guidance, directly marking the contrary response anticipated by the focus.
The magicians refuse Pharaoh after receiving clear proofs, demonstrating a concrete response to signs within the same narrative.
The messenger's command to be first in submission offers a general obedience parallel.
It joins a requested sign with the possibility of being gathered upon guidance, but remains a different setting.
It links opposing the messenger after guidance becomes clear with the nullification of deeds, a later counterpart to the focus's warning.
The messenger's roles as witness, bearer of good news, and warner provide broad context for Musa and Harun's commission.
Pharaoh's dispatch of gatherers is a coercive counter-action to the liberation movement demanded in the focus.
The command to worship and establish prayer supplies the wider divine authority, but not the specific Pharaoh address.
It directly pairs security with being rightly guided, supporting the focus's association of peace and following guidance.
The pilgrimage regulations and sacrificial offering do not clarify the focus's messenger, liberation, or guidance themes.
It makes obedience to the messenger the route to guidance and defines the messenger's duty as clear delivery.
The detailed debt-writing procedure has no focused relation to the mission before Pharaoh.
The inability to guide one whom God has left astray is a distant boundary case for the focus's guidance language.
Obedience to what the messenger gives is a general authority parallel, but adds no specific insight into Musa's demand.
A sound heart before God only loosely relates to the focus's peace and guidance.
The isolated command to cast the staff does not explain the focus after the surrounding mission and sign texts are already represented.
The revelation to Musa's mother that he will become a messenger gives background for the messenger identity asserted in the focus.
Those expelled unjustly for confessing God provide a broader counterpart to liberation from oppressive power and religious coercion.
Sending a destructive flood after people turn away is a distant consequence parallel to rejecting divine direction.
Musa directly identifies himself to Pharaoh as a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, supplying the commission asserted in the focus.
Musa casts his staff before Pharaoh as a manifest sign, concretizing the sign brought from the Lord in the focus.
The shining hand is a second manifest sign in the same confrontation with Pharaoh.
It explicitly recalls rescue from Pharaoh's people, who inflicted grievous torment on the Children of Israel.
Musa and Harun are sent to Pharaoh and his chiefs with God's signs, closely matching the joint mission in the focus.
It shows that fear of Pharaoh's persecution constrained even those who believed in Musa, clarifying the danger behind the request not to torment Israel.
Musa calls his people to trust God if they have submitted, supplying the community-side response to the mission.
Pharaoh's final attempted belief after pursuing the Children of Israel gives the narrative outcome of rejecting the earlier guidance.
It explicitly joins Musa, Pharaoh, and nine clear signs, providing a direct account of the proof-bearing confrontation.
Pharaoh's intent to drive the Children of Israel from the land, followed by his drowning, reverses the coercive power challenged in the focus.
The command for the Children of Israel to dwell in the land states the post-Pharaoh freedom that the focus seeks.
The command to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed begins the commission later verbalized in the focus.
God's granting of Musa's request confirms the preparation that makes the paired mission of the focus possible.
Pharaoh's question about the Lord opens his direct response to the messengers' claim in the focus.
Revelation to Musa to travel by night with God's servants gives the enacted departure demanded from Pharaoh in the focus.
God addresses the Children of Israel as saved from their enemy, naming the realized safety behind the focus's appeal.
The command to go to the wrongdoing people of Pharaoh is a direct antecedent to the focus's confrontation.
God reassures Musa and Harun that He is hearing with them, leading into their joint approach to Pharaoh.
The instruction to travel by night with God's servants directly enacts the release of the Children of Israel.
Pharaoh and his forces follow at sunrise, making visible the coercive response to Israel's departure.
The sea's parting enables the escape of the people whose release is demanded in the focus.
The saving of Musa and all who were with him gives the mission's decisive protective outcome.
The staff and hand signs are explicitly described as proofs for Pharaoh and his chiefs.
God strengthens Musa through Harun and grants both authority, so Pharaoh's party cannot reach them through the signs.
Musa is sent to Pharaoh, Haman, and Korah with God's signs and clear authority.
Musa's declaration of being a messenger from the Lord of the worlds closely parallels the focus's self-identification.
Pharaoh's order to kill the sons of those who believe with Musa exposes the persecution opposed by the focus's prohibition of torment.
Musa's sending to Pharaoh and his chiefs with God's signs provides another direct statement of the mission.
The signs shown to Pharaoh's court make their hostile reaction to divine proof explicit.
The command to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed directly parallels the commissioning context of the focus.
Musa's invitation to purification provides a closely related formulation of Pharaoh's offered path of reform.
Musa offers to guide Pharaoh to his Lord so that he may fear, directly expanding the focus's call to follow guidance.
Musa shows Pharaoh the great sign, directly corresponding to the focus's claim to bring a sign from the Lord.
Pharaoh's denial and disobedience give the contrary response warned against in the focus.
